primitives.name: Monge problem: move a measure by a deterministic map that pushes the source mass exactly onto the target
primitives.verbatim_quote: the Monge problem [1781] seeks a map that associates to each point xi a single point yj and which must push the mass of α toward the mass of β
primitives.page: Sec. 2.2, Remark 2.4, Eq. (2.5), printed p. 9-11, text line ~451

symbol_and_unit_ledger.c(x_i, T(x_i)): ground cost of moving the mass at source point x_i to its image T(x_i) [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.T: transport map from source support points to target support points [dimensionless assignment]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.alpha, beta: source and target discrete measures; T_sharp alpha = beta is exact mass conservation under the map

assumptions: A map must exist: the target weights must be exactly representable as sums of source weights, which fails whenever the target support is larger than the source support.
Each source point sends all of its mass to a single target point; no mass splitting is allowed.
The feasible set of push-forward maps is nonconvex, so the problem is hard to solve in this form.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Infeasible for generic discrete measures (no map exists when weights are incompatible, e.g. more target points than source points); nonconvex and combinatorial in the assignment special case with n! permutations.

layer2.mapping: The Monge form is the engine's deterministic reassignment operator: a rule that moves an entire probability distribution of outcomes from one state to another while conserving total probability mass exactly. It is the formal skeleton behind any counterfactual of the form: take the observed distribution of a unit's plays and push it through a known transformation, such as a scheme change or a personnel swap, to obtain the distribution that unit would produce under the new condition.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical distributions over plays, drives, or possessions with their support points (field position, down, distance, formation) and weights (observed frequencies).

primitives.name: Kantorovich relaxation: replace the deterministic map with a coupling matrix that may split mass, giving a linear program over the transportation polytope
primitives.verbatim_quote: Kantorovich proposes instead that the mass at any point xi be potentially dispatched across several locations
primitives.page: Sec. 2.3, Eqs. (2.10)-(2.11), printed p. 13-14, text line ~630
primitives.latex: L_C(a,b) = \min_{P \in U(a,b)} \langle C, P \rangle, \quad U(a,b) = \{P \in \mathbb{R}_+^{n \times m} : P\mathbf{1}_m = a,\ P^{\top}\mathbf{1}_n = b\}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P_{i,j}: amount of mass transported from source bin i to target bin j [probability mass]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.C_{i,j}: unit cost of moving mass from bin i to bin j [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.a, b: source and target histograms in the probability simplices [probability mass]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.U(a,b): transportation polytope: all nonnegative matrices with row sums a and column sums b

assumptions: Both histograms have the same total mass (both lie in probability simplices).
Cost is linear in the amount of mass moved: shipping a units from i to j costs a times C_{i,j}.
Mass is infinitely divisible, so fractional plans are admissible.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Requires equal total mass on both sides; the linear cost ignores congestion or interaction effects; the optimum need not be unique; a dense coupling is harder to interpret as an actual reassignment than a map.

layer2.mapping: The coupling is the engine's soft matching object: instead of forcing a one-to-one assignment between two distributions (for example this week's play distribution and a historical baseline), the engine keeps the full matrix of how much mass moves from each source state to each target state. Row and column sums are hard conservation constraints, so any downstream quantity computed from the coupling automatically respects the observed totals on both sides.
layer2.telemetry: Two histograms on a shared state space: play-type frequencies, target-share distributions, snap distributions by personnel grouping, with a cost matrix between states.

primitives.name: For uniform histograms of equal size the Kantorovich relaxation is tight: some optimal coupling is a permutation matrix (Birkhoff's theorem)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Birkhoff’s theorem [1946] states that the set of extremal points of U(1n /n, 1n /n) is equal to the set of permutation matrices
primitives.page: Sec. 2.3, Proposition 2.1, printed p. 15, text line ~731

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P_sigma: permutation coupling matrix scaled by 1/n [probability mass]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of bins, equal on both sides

assumptions: Both histograms are uniform (every weight equals 1/n) and have the same number of bins n = m.
The linear program attains its minimum at an extremal point of the polytope.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Tightness fails as a guarantee for nonuniform weights: with general histograms an optimal coupling may genuinely need to split mass, and no permutation need be optimal.

layer2.mapping: This is the certificate the engine uses when it solves a relaxed matching but reports a hard assignment: when the two sides are uniform empirical samples of the same size, the relaxation loses nothing, so an optimal one-to-one pairing (player to player, play to play, drive to drive) always exists among the optimal soft plans and can be extracted without changing the optimal cost.
layer2.telemetry: Equal-size empirical samples: two sets of n plays, n drives, or n player-game lines to be paired one-to-one.

primitives.name: With a power of a ground distance as cost, the optimal transport value is a true metric on histograms and measures: the p-Wasserstein distance lifts the ground geometry
primitives.verbatim_quote: OT can be understood as a canonical way to lift a ground distance between points to a distance between histogram or measures
primitives.page: Sec. 2.4, Propositions 2.2-2.3, Eqs. (2.17)-(2.18), printed p. 19-21, text line ~883

symbol_and_unit_ledger.D: ground distance matrix between bins [distance units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_{D^p}: optimal transport value with cost matrix D raised elementwise to the power p
symbol_and_unit_ledger.W_p: p-Wasserstein distance between the histograms [distance units]

assumptions: The cost matrix is the p-th power of a genuine distance: symmetric, zero diagonal, triangle inequality.
The triangle inequality for W_p is proved by gluing two optimal couplings through their shared marginal.
primitives.breakdown_regime: If the cost is not a power of a metric (arbitrary substitution costs), the value is a transport cost but not a distance: symmetry, definiteness, or the triangle inequality can fail. For 0 < p <= 1 it is W_p^p, not W_p, that is a distance.

layer2.mapping: The lifting property is what licenses the engine to turn any pointwise dissimilarity it trusts (distance between two plays, two routes, two field positions) into a principled distance between whole distributions of those objects, with metric guarantees: identical distributions score zero, the score is symmetric, and chained comparisons obey the triangle inequality, so distribution distances can be composed and audited like ordinary distances.
layer2.telemetry: A ground distance on the state space (play embeddings, field coordinates, route shapes) plus empirical histograms over that space for each team, unit, or player.

primitives.name: Wasserstein distance metrizes weak convergence: it compares even singular, non-overlapping distributions and reduces to the ground distance between two point masses
primitives.verbatim_quote: it allows one to compare singular distributions (for instance, discrete ones) whose supports do not overlap and to quantify the spatial shift between the supports of two distributions
primitives.page: Sec. 2.4, Remark 2.18 and Definition 2.2, printed p. 21-22, text line ~1018

symbol_and_unit_ledger.delta_x: Dirac mass concentrated at point x [probability measure]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.d(x, y): ground distance between the two support points [distance units]

assumptions: Convergence in W_p is equivalent to weak convergence plus convergence of moments of order p on unbounded spaces.
The ground space carries a genuine distance d.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Divergences such as Kullback-Leibler or total variation cannot do this: they are infinite or maximal between disjoint supports. W_infinity is a nonconvex exception in the family and is hard to compute.

layer2.mapping: This is the property that makes Wasserstein the engine's default discrepancy for sparse empirical data: two players or teams whose observed plays never land in exactly the same states still get a finite, graded distance that grows smoothly as their distributions shift apart in space, instead of the all-or-nothing verdict a density-ratio divergence would give. Single observations also embed exactly, since the distance between two point masses is just their ground distance.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical play or tracking distributions with disjoint or barely overlapping supports; sequences of weekly distributions whose convergence or drift is being monitored.

primitives.name: Kantorovich duality: the transport cost equals a maximization over price potentials f and g constrained by f_i + g_j <= C_{i,j} on every pair
primitives.verbatim_quote: The Kantorovich problem (2.11) is a constrained convex minimization problem, and as such, it can be naturally paired with a so-called dual problem, which is a constrained concave maximization problem
primitives.page: Sec. 2.5, Proposition 2.4, Eqs. (2.20)-(2.21), printed p. 23, text line ~1073
primitives.latex: L_C(a,b) = \max_{(f,g) \in R(C)} \langle f, a \rangle + \langle g, b \rangle, \quad R(C) = \{(f,g) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m : f \oplus g \le C\}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_i: dual potential (collection price) at source bin i [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.g_j: dual potential (delivery price) at target bin j [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f oplus g: matrix with entries f_i + g_j [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.R(C): set of admissible potential pairs, one inequality per source-target pair

assumptions: Strong duality holds because the primal is a finite-dimensional linear program.
Potentials are defined only up to an additive constant shift (f + t, g - t) that leaves the objective unchanged.
primitives.breakdown_regime: For arbitrary measures, existence of optimal potentials is nontrivial because the constraint set is not compact; for the entropic problem the potentials lose their automatic Lipschitz regularity.

layer2.mapping: Duality gives the engine an attribution layer for free: the optimal potentials price every source state and every target state, so a distribution comparison decomposes into which states are expensive to empty and which are expensive to fill. A feasible potential pair also certifies a lower bound on the true distance without solving the full transport problem, which is a cheap audit the engine can run before trusting any approximate solver output.
layer2.telemetry: The cost matrix and histograms of the comparison being priced; the resulting potential vectors per state (formation, field zone, route concept).

primitives.name: Complementary slackness: mass only flows on pairs where the potentials saturate the cost, f_i + g_j = C_{i,j}; the optimal plan's support is located by the dual solution
primitives.verbatim_quote: The primal-dual optimality relation for the Lagrangian (2.22) allows us to locate the support of the optimal transport plan
primitives.page: Sec. 2.5 Eq. (2.23) and Sec. 3.3 Propositions 3.2-3.3, printed p. 23 and p. 41, text line ~1109

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_i + g_j: combined dual price of the pair [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.C_{i,j}: unit transport cost of the pair [cost units]

assumptions: The primal and dual solutions are both optimal (strong duality holds).
Feasibility plus complementarity is also sufficient: any feasible primal-dual pair satisfying the condition is optimal.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The condition characterizes optimal pairs but does not by itself construct them; degenerate problems can have many optimal plans sharing the same saturated set.

layer2.mapping: Complementary slackness is the engine's consistency check between a proposed matching and its price explanation: any pair carrying flow must be exactly priced, and any underpriced pair must carry none. In reasoning terms it separates the active correspondences (the pairs the optimal plan actually uses, which are exactly the tight constraints) from the inactive background, so explanations can cite only the binding pairs.
layer2.telemetry: A candidate coupling and candidate potentials from any solver; the set of tight pairs is the auditable explanation of the plan.

primitives.name: Brenier theorem: for the squared Euclidean cost with a density on the source, the optimal coupling is unique, is a Monge map, and that map is the gradient of a convex function
primitives.verbatim_quote: Furthermore, this map T is uniquely defined as the gradient of a convex function ϕ, T (x) = ∇ϕ(x), where ϕ is the unique (up to an additive constant) convex function
primitives.page: Sec. 2.5, Remark 2.24, Theorem 2.1, printed p. 27-28, text line ~1285

symbol_and_unit_ledger.varphi: Brenier potential, a convex function [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f: Kantorovich dual potential for the squared cost [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.nabla varphi: gradient map, monotone by convexity of varphi

assumptions: Ground space is R^d and the cost is the squared Euclidean distance.
At least one of the two measures has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure; both have finite second moments.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails without a density: purely discrete sources can require mass splitting, and for p = 1 or metric costs the optimal coupling is generally not unique and no such map need exist. Regularity of the map can break down for irregular target supports.

layer2.mapping: Brenier's theorem is the structural license for treating an optimal distributional shift as a single well-defined transformation: when the source distribution is continuous, there is exactly one optimal way to morph it into the target, and that morph is monotone in the strong sense of being a convex gradient. For the engine this justifies interpolating distributions along the optimal path and reading the map itself, not just its cost, as the explanation of how one state of a unit becomes another.
layer2.telemetry: Continuous or finely discretized distributions over tracking space or play embeddings, where a density approximation of the source is defensible.

primitives.name: The Brenier potential solves a Monge-Ampère equation: the Jacobian determinant of the map, weighted by the target density at the image, reproduces the source density
primitives.verbatim_quote: one obtains that ϕ is the unique (up to the addition of a constant) convex function which solves the following Monge–Ampère-type equation
primitives.page: Sec. 2.5, Remark 2.25, Eq. (2.32), printed p. 29, text line ~1360

symbol_and_unit_ledger.partial^2 varphi(x): Hessian matrix of the Brenier potential at x [dimensionless curvature]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho_alpha, rho_beta: source and target densities [probability per unit volume]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.det: Jacobian determinant of the map, the local volume change factor

assumptions: Both measures have densities and the optimal map is smooth and bijective.
Convexity of the potential enforces a nonnegative determinant, which is necessary for a solution to exist.
primitives.breakdown_regime: In full generality solutions need not be smooth (Alexandrov weak solutions are required), the equation is a nonlinear degenerate elliptic PDE, and its discretization with the density depending on the map's own gradient is numerically delicate.

layer2.mapping: The Monge-Ampère form turns distribution matching into a local conservation law the engine can check pointwise: wherever the map compresses volume, the target density must be proportionally higher. It is the differential version of mass conservation, useful as a diagnostic residual: regions where the equation is violated are regions where a proposed transformation of one distribution into another is not mass-consistent.
layer2.telemetry: Density estimates of source and target over a continuous state space, plus the Jacobian of a candidate transformation between them.

primitives.name: In one dimension everything is closed form: W_p is the L^p distance between quantile functions, W_1 is the L^1 distance between CDFs, and the optimal map composes one CDF with the other's quantile function
primitives.verbatim_quote: This means that through the map α 7→ Cα−1 , the Wasserstein distance is isometric to a linear space equipped with the Lp norm
primitives.page: Sec. 2.6, Remarks 2.28-2.30, Eqs. (2.33)-(2.39), printed p. 30-32, text line ~1493
primitives.latex: W_p(\alpha, \beta)^p = \int_0^1 |C_\alpha^{-1}(r) - C_\beta^{-1}(r)|^p \, dr, \quad T = C_\beta^{-1} \circ C_\alpha

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C_alpha^{-1}: generalized inverse CDF (quantile function) [units of the variable]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.T: monotone optimal transport map on the real line

assumptions: The ground space is the real line and the cost is a power of the absolute distance.
Atoms are matched in sorted order (monotone rearrangement); distinctness of points is assumed for the local formula.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The isometry is special to dimension one; in higher dimensions the Wasserstein space is not Hilbertian (Sec. 8.3). Concave costs (p < 1) change the structure of optimal plans.

layer2.mapping: The 1-D formulas are the engine's fast lane for scalar distributions: yards gained, air yards, time to pressure, EPA per play. Any such distribution is summarized exactly by its quantile curve, distances become plain L^p distances between curves, and the optimal map is a monotone recalibration, so a player's distribution can be warped onto a baseline by composing CDFs with no optimization solver at all.
layer2.telemetry: Scalar per-play or per-game measurements with their empirical CDFs and quantile functions at a grid of probability levels.

primitives.name: Between Gaussians, W_2 has a closed form: squared mean gap plus the Bures metric between covariances, with an explicit linear optimal map
primitives.verbatim_quote: where B is the so-called Bures metric [1969] between positive definite matrices
primitives.page: Sec. 2.6, Remark 2.31, Eqs. (2.40)-(2.42), printed p. 33-34, text line ~1594

symbol_and_unit_ledger.m_alpha, m_beta: mean vectors of the two Gaussians [units of the variable]

assumptions: Both measures are Gaussian (the formula extends to elliptically contoured families with the same generator, up to a scaling of the Bures term).
The optimal map is affine: x maps to m_beta + A(x - m_alpha) with A symmetric positive definite.
primitives.breakdown_regime: For non-Gaussian measures the Gaussian-to-Gaussian distance is only a lower bound on the true distance (Gelbrich bound); using it as the distance itself understates discrepancy whenever shape beyond second moments matters.

layer2.mapping: The Bures closed form lets the engine compare summarized units exactly when a Gaussian summary is honest: a team's per-play outcome distribution compressed to a mean vector and covariance gets an exact W_2, decomposed additively into a location part (mean gap) and a shape part (covariance mismatch), and the same formula supplies the exact average (barycenter) of several such summaries through its fixed point.
layer2.telemetry: Mean vectors and covariance matrices of multivariate per-play features (yards, EPA, field position) per team, unit, or player.

primitives.name: The c-transform collapses the dual problem to a single potential: given f, the best partner is g = f^C, and applying the transform pair twice is idempotent, so alternation plateaus
primitives.verbatim_quote: there is no better vector solution for g than the C-transform vector of f, denoted f C ∈ Rm
primitives.page: Sec. 3.2, Eq. (3.5) and Proposition 3.1, printed p. 40-41, text line ~1842

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f^C: C-transform of the source potentials, the largest feasible partner vector [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.C_{i,j} - f_i: slack-adjusted cost of pairing source i with target j [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f^{C bar-C}: double transform, the c-concave envelope of f

assumptions: The dual constraints are exactly f_i + g_j <= C_{i,j} for all pairs.
Idempotence f^{CCbarC} = f^C is a property of the exact (hard-min) transform; the entropic soft-min version is not idempotent, which is precisely why Sinkhorn alternation keeps moving.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Alternating exact transforms cannot be used as a solver: after one round trip the potentials stop improving even though they may not yet be optimal. The transform is also nonsmooth, which blocks direct gradient methods in the unregularized problem.

layer2.mapping: The c-transform is the engine's best-response operator for prices: given valuations on one side of a comparison, it computes the most aggressive feasible valuations on the other side in one min-plus pass. Its idempotence is a warning the engine encodes as doctrine: a single best-response round is not convergence, so any iterative pricing scheme must add smoothing (the entropic soft-min) or another mechanism to keep improving.
layer2.telemetry: Potential vectors on states and the pairwise cost matrix; min-plus (tropical) matrix-vector products over the state space.

primitives.name: Extremal optimal plans are sparse and acyclic: a vertex of the transportation polytope has at most n + m - 1 nonzero entries and its support graph is a forest
primitives.verbatim_quote: All NW corner solutions have by construction up to n + m − 1 nonzero elements
primitives.page: Sec. 3.4, Proposition 3.4 and Sec. 3.4.2, printed p. 42-45, text line ~2104

symbol_and_unit_ledger.n, m: numbers of source and target bins [count]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P_{i,j} > 0: pairs carrying positive flow in the plan [probability mass]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.support graph: bipartite graph on n + m nodes whose edges are the positive entries

assumptions: An optimal vertex exists because the feasible polytope is bounded and the objective is linear.
A support containing a cycle can always be perturbed in both directions along the cycle, so it cannot be extremal.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Sparsity is a property of vertices, not of every optimal plan: entropic regularization deliberately returns dense plans, and degenerate problems admit dense optimal plans too. The north-west corner rule reaches only a subset of vertices.

layer2.mapping: Vertex sparsity bounds how complicated an exact explanation can be: an optimal hard matching between two histograms never needs more than n + m - 1 active links, and those links form a forest, so the engine can present an exact optimal reassignment as a small set of trees rather than a dense matrix. It also gives a compression target: any plan with a cycle in its support can be simplified without changing its marginals.
layer2.telemetry: Support size and cycle structure of computed couplings between histograms on n source and m target states.

primitives.name: Network simplex: maintain a spanning-tree plan and its complementary potentials, add the most violated dual constraint as an edge, pivot flow around the created cycle until no violation remains
primitives.verbatim_quote: The network simplex algorithm can therefore be summarized as follows: Initialize the algorithm with an extremal solution P, given for instance by the NW corner rule
primitives.page: Sec. 3.5, printed p. 45-48, text line ~2271
assumptions: Starts from a feasible vertex (for instance from the north-west corner rule) whose support graph is a forest.
Potentials complementary to the current tree are recovered by rooting each tree and traversing it, fixing one free potential per component.
Each pivot either strictly decreases the transport cost or is degenerate (changes only the tree, not the plan).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Worst-case behavior depends on the pivot rule; polynomiality was only proved with specific pivot strategies (Orlin), and degenerate pivots can stall progress on the plan itself. Exact LP solvers are outclassed by Sinkhorn-type iterations when only an approximate distance is needed.

layer2.mapping: The network simplex is the engine's exact solver of record for small and medium matchings where a certificate matters: it returns not just a plan but complementary potentials proving optimality, and its tree representation keeps the active correspondence human-auditable. The engine reserves it for cases where an approximate entropic answer would not be defensible, and uses its potentials as ground truth to validate faster approximate solvers.
layer2.telemetry: Cost matrices of moderate size (hundreds to thousands of states per side) where exactness is required, plus the tree and potentials the solver maintains.

primitives.name: Auction algorithm: unassigned sources bid for targets by raising the winner's price by the gap between best and second-best adjusted costs plus epsilon, guaranteeing an assignment within n*epsilon of optimal
primitives.verbatim_quote: The number of steps of the auction algorithm is at most N = nkCk∞ /ε
primitives.page: Sec. 3.7, Eqs. (3.8)-(3.9) and Propositions 3.7-3.9, printed p. 53-56, text line ~2614

symbol_and_unit_ledger.j_i^1, j_i^2: targets with the smallest and second-smallest adjusted costs C_{i,j} - g_j for bidder i
symbol_and_unit_ledger.g_j: current price (dual variable) of target j [cost units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon: minimum bid increment [cost units]; final assignment is at most n*epsilon suboptimal
symbol_and_unit_ledger.||C||_infty: largest absolute entry of the cost matrix [cost units]

assumptions: Solves the assignment problem: uniform histograms with n = m.
Maintains epsilon-complementary slackness throughout; prices only ever move in one direction, which bounds the iteration count.
Epsilon-scaling (restarting with decreasing epsilon) reduces the naive complexity to near O(n^3 log ||C||_infty).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Native form handles only the balanced assignment case; a fixed epsilon trades accuracy for speed, and a poor epsilon schedule wastes iterations. Extension to general histograms requires reformulation.

layer2.mapping: The auction is the engine's market mechanism for one-to-one matching under contention: when several source items want the same target (the same defender, the same coverage shell, the same role), prices adjust until contention resolves, and the n*epsilon bound states exactly how far the resulting assignment can be from optimal. It is the formal version of letting contested assignments settle by bidding rather than by central fiat.
layer2.telemetry: Assignment problems between equal-size sets with a cost matrix and observed contention (multiple sources preferring the same target).

primitives.name: Entropic regularization: subtracting epsilon times the entropy makes the transport problem strongly convex with a unique solution, which is the Kullback-Leibler projection of the Gibbs kernel exp(-C/epsilon) onto the coupling polytope
primitives.verbatim_quote: Since the objective is an ε-strongly convex function, Problem (4.2) has a unique optimal solution
primitives.page: Sec. 4.1, Eqs. (4.1)-(4.7) and Proposition 4.1, printed p. 57-60, text line ~2692
primitives.latex: L_C^\varepsilon(a,b) = \min_{P \in U(a,b)} \langle P, C \rangle - \varepsilon H(P), \quad K = e^{-C/\varepsilon}, \quad P^\varepsilon = \mathrm{Proj}^{KL}_{U(a,b)}(K)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon: regularization strength [cost units]; controls the blur of the plan
symbol_and_unit_ledger.H(P): discrete entropy of the coupling, -sum P_{i,j} (log P_{i,j} - 1) [nats]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Proj^KL: projection in Kullback-Leibler divergence onto the marginal constraints

assumptions: Entropy is 1-strongly concave, so the regularized objective is epsilon-strongly convex and the optimizer is unique.
As epsilon tends to 0 the solution converges to the maximum-entropy optimal plan of the original problem; as epsilon tends to infinity it converges to the independence coupling a b^T.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The regularized value is a biased estimate of the true transport cost and the plan is dense rather than sparse; small epsilon restores accuracy but destroys numerical stability and convergence speed.

layer2.mapping: Entropic regularization is the engine's master dial between a sharp explanation and a smooth statistic: positive epsilon turns a brittle combinatorial matching into a differentiable, uniquely defined comparison that can sit inside a larger optimization (fitting a model by minimizing transport loss), at the documented price of bias that Sec. 8.5 later corrects. Every use must report its epsilon, because the number is meaningless without it.
layer2.telemetry: Cost matrices and histograms; the entropy of computed couplings as a diagnostic of how diffuse the plan is at the chosen epsilon.

primitives.name: Sinkhorn's algorithm: the regularized optimum factors as diag(u) K diag(v), and alternating row and column rescalings u = a/(Kv), v = b/(K^T u) solve it with only matrix-vector products
primitives.verbatim_quote: That problem is known in the numerical analysis community as the matrix scaling problem
primitives.page: Sec. 4.2, Proposition 4.3 and Eqs. (4.12)-(4.15), printed p. 63-64, text line ~3050

symbol_and_unit_ledger.u, v: positive scaling vectors [dimensionless], defined up to a reciprocal multiplicative constant
symbol_and_unit_ledger.a/(Kv): entrywise division of the target row sums by the current row sums [dimensionless]

assumptions: First-order optimality of the entropic problem forces the factored form of the solution.
Each half-iteration enforces one marginal exactly; convergence to the joint solution is proved via the Hilbert metric contraction (Theorem 4.2).
Iterations for many histogram pairs batch into matrix-matrix products, which is the GPU-friendly form.
primitives.breakdown_regime: For small epsilon the kernel entries underflow to zero in floating point and the divisions break down; the raw iterations must then be replaced by the log-domain form. Each iteration costs O(nm) unless the kernel has exploitable structure (separability, convolution, heat kernel).

layer2.mapping: Sinkhorn is the engine's workhorse comparator: it prices the discrepancy between two distributions using nothing but repeated rescalings, runs identically on one comparison or a batch of thousands, and its intermediate scalings double as potentials. Because the updates are matrix products against a kernel, the kernel itself becomes the modeling choice: encode the ground geometry once, and every comparison inherits it.
layer2.telemetry: Gibbs kernel evaluations from the ground cost, batches of histogram pairs (team-week distributions, player distributions), GPU matrix products.

primitives.breakdown_regime: Choosing tau is choosing how much of the discrepancy is explained by moving mass versus creating or destroying it; too small a tau lets the plan ignore geometry and just delete hard-to-move mass. Renormalizing inputs to fake balance is the common wrong shortcut the formalism exists to replace.

layer2.mapping: Unbalanced OT is the engine's comparison for objects whose totals legitimately differ: rosters change, snap counts change, a unit plays more or fewer plays, mass appears and disappears. Instead of normalizing those facts away, the engine prices them: tau states the exchange rate between transporting mass and writing it off, and the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao instance gives a true metric on unnormalized measures for cases where the total itself is signal.
layer2.telemetry: Histograms with unequal totals (snap shares across weeks with different play counts, roster distributions across seasons), plus a documented tau per comparison.

primitives.name: Sliced Wasserstein: average the closed-form 1-D Wasserstein distances of all one-dimensional projections; computable by sorting, negative definite, and the basis of positive definite transport kernels
primitives.verbatim_quote: One can define a distance between two measures (α, β) defined on Rd by aggregating 1-D Wasserstein distances between their projections onto all directions of the sphere
primitives.page: Sec. 10.4, Eq. (10.13), printed p. 166-168, text line ~7743

symbol_and_unit_ledger.theta: unit direction on the sphere S^d [dimensionless]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P_{theta sharp} alpha: push-forward of alpha under projection onto direction theta, a 1-D measure
symbol_and_unit_ledger.W_2 in 1-D: computed by sorting and the quantile formula of Sec. 2.6 [distance units]

assumptions: Each projected problem is one-dimensional, so each term is exact and cheap; in practice the integral is Monte Carlo over random directions.
As a sum of negative definite functions, the sliced distance is negative definite, enabling positive definite kernels of the form exp(-SW^p / t).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Slicing loses information: distinct multivariate distributions can share many projections, the Monte Carlo estimate adds variance that shrinks only with the number of directions, and the sliced value is a lower bound style surrogate, not the true Wasserstein distance, with no coupling or map between the original measures.

layer2.mapping: Sliced Wasserstein is the engine's scalable screening distance for high-dimensional distributions: project play or tracking embeddings onto random directions, sort, and accumulate exact 1-D costs. It trades the full coupling for speed and kernel validity, and the engine uses it where a ranking of discrepancies or a positive definite kernel is needed, reserving full transport for the finalists that need a map and an explanation.
layer2.telemetry: High-dimensional empirical distributions, a direction budget (number of random projections), and sorted projected samples per direction.

primitives.name: Gromov-Wasserstein compares metric measure spaces intrinsically: minimize the distortion of pairwise distances under a coupling, with no shared ground space; the problem is a nonconvex quadratic assignment, attacked by entropic mirror descent with Sinkhorn inner loops
primitives.verbatim_quote: Optimal transport needs a ground cost C to compare histograms (a, b) and thus cannot be used if the bins of those histograms are not defined on the same underlying space

symbol_and_unit_ledger.D, D': intra-space distance (or similarity) matrices of the two objects [distance units]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P_{i,j} P_{i',j'}: joint probability that i maps to j and i' maps to j' [probability mass squared]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.distortion: squared mismatch between the two internal distances of a matched pair of pairs

assumptions: Each object is described only by its internal pairwise distances and a probability distribution over its points (a metric measure space).
GW is a distance between such spaces up to measure-preserving isometry: it vanishes exactly for intrinsically identical structures.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Nonconvex and NP-hard in general (equivalent to quadratic assignment and graph matching); entropic mirror descent finds only stationary points whose quality depends on initialization, and the objective costs O(n^2 m^2) naively. It answers structural similarity, not a transport plan between shared states.

layer2.mapping: Gromov-Wasserstein is the engine's cross-domain comparator: when two objects live in different spaces with no honest pointwise cost (two teams' play graphs, a college and a pro player's route tree, formations across eras), it compares their internal geometries and returns the soft correspondence that least distorts pairwise relationships. The returned correspondence is used as a hypothesis generator for structural analogies, never as evidence that the spaces are the same.
layer2.telemetry: Internal distance matrices of two structures (play-type similarity graphs, route networks, formation graphs) with node weights, plus multi-start entropic GW runs to probe stationary-point stability.

reasoning_traces.think: This monograph is the computational turn of a two-hundred-year-old idea. Monge asked how to move a pile of earth onto a target shape with the least work when each grain must travel whole; Kantorovich relaxed the question by letting mass split, and that single relaxation converts a nonconvex, often infeasible problem into a linear program whose geometry, duality, and algorithms the rest of the book unfolds. The architecture is deliberate. First the objects: histograms, discrete measures, arbitrary measures, couplings as joint distributions with prescribed marginals. Then the value: with a power of a ground distance as cost, the optimal value is the Wasserstein distance, a true metric that lifts the geometry of the ground space to the space of distributions and metrizes weak convergence, so even disjoint empirical samples sit at a finite, graded distance. Then duality: every transport problem has a shadow price system, the Kantorovich potentials, and complementary slackness ties the plan to the prices so tightly that each explains the other. Brenier's theorem closes the theoretical arc for the squared Euclidean cost: with a density present, relaxation loses nothing, the optimal plan is a single map, and that map is the gradient of a convex function solving a Monge-Ampère equation, which is why optimal transport doubles as a theory of multivariate quantiles. The second half of the book is about what to do when the exact machinery is too slow or too brittle. Classical solvers (network simplex, dual ascent, auction) exploit the polytope's sparse tree-structured vertices. Entropic regularization then trades a controlled amount of bias for a strongly convex problem whose solution factors through a Gibbs kernel and is computable by Sinkhorn's rescaling iterations, analyzable exactly through the Hilbert projective contraction, stabilizable in the log domain, and differentiable, which is what admits transport into variational problems: barycenters as Frechet means of distributions, gradient flows whose implicit steps are Wasserstein proximal steps, and minimum Kantorovich estimators that fit generative models likelihood methods cannot touch. The statistical chapters supply the discipline: phi-divergences see only overlap, MMD sees only kernel geometry, empirical Wasserstein converges at a dimension-cursed rate, and the debiased Sinkhorn divergence interpolates deliberately between transport geometry and kernel statistics as epsilon varies. The extensions relax the founding assumptions one at a time: unequal mass (unbalanced OT and the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric), many marginals (tensor couplings, with barycenters as a corollary), cheap high-dimensional surrogates (sliced Wasserstein built from the closed-form one-dimensional theory), and incomparable spaces (Gromov-Wasserstein, which compares internal distance structures and pays for it with nonconvexity). For a reasoning engine, the book's real export is a complete, auditable stack for the operation 'compare two distributions honestly.' Every level carries its own certificate and its own warning. Duality certifies bounds and attributes cost to states through potentials. Complementary slackness certifies that a plan and its price explanation agree. The contraction theory certifies Sinkhorn accuracy from marginal violations instead of iteration counts. The sample complexity results veto overconfident readings of small samples in high dimensions. The non-Hilbertian result vetoes a whole family of plausible kernel constructions. The epsilon parameter is never a nuisance to hide: it is a declared modeling choice that moves the answer between geometry and statistics, and the book insists on correcting its bias when reporting distances. Where the machinery breaks is equally explicit: mass conservation is a real constraint that reality often violates, which is why the unbalanced theory exists; one-dimensional and Gaussian closed forms are seductive exceptions that do not survive contact with general multivariate data; small epsilon is exponentially expensive; and Gromov-Wasserstein buys cross-domain comparison at the price of NP-hard nonconvexity, so its outputs are hypotheses, not measurements. A system that internalizes both halves, the operators and their failure envelopes, can compare distributions as a routine, explainable operation rather than as a leap of faith. The middle chapters deserve attention as a study in how structure becomes computation. The transportation polytope's vertices are forests with at most n + m - 1 edges, so exact optimal plans are sparse enough to draw, and the network simplex is nothing but disciplined walking on those trees, guided by potentials that must agree with the plan on every used edge. The c-transform shows the dual problem secretly has half its apparent degrees of freedom, and its idempotence explains why naive alternation stalls, a small theorem with large consequences because the entropic smoothing of exactly that transform is what makes Sinkhorn alternation converge instead. The semidiscrete chapter turns duality into geometry: one continuous measure against finitely many targets is a tessellation problem, the Laguerre cells are the regions each target serves, and the gradient of the whole problem is just the vector of cell-mass errors, which is as interpretable as an optimization signal ever gets. The dynamic chapter changes the question from where mass goes to how it flows, and the momentum change of variables that convexifies Benamou-Brenier is a reminder that the right coordinates can matter more than the right solver. Even the one-dimensional and Gaussian closed forms pull weight far beyond their special cases: they anchor intuition, they supply the sliced distances used at scale, and the Bures geometry reappears inside barycenters of Gaussians and inside the fixed points used to average covariance structure. Read as a whole, the book argues that a distance between distributions is not a number but a small theory: a ground cost that states what movement means, a conservation law that states what must be accounted for, a dual price system that states who pays, a plan that states what actually moves, and a set of theorems stating when each of those objects exists, is unique, is computable, and is statistically meaningful. Systems that adopt only the number inherit the failure modes the book documents: bias mistaken for signal, sparsity demanded where the geometry forbids it, kernel methods applied where no embedding exists, certainty claimed where the sampling rate forbids it. Systems that adopt the whole stack gain something rarer than a metric, namely a disciplined way to disagree with their own computations, because every transport answer arrives with the potentials, residuals, and rates needed to cross-examine it.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs Monge's 1781 earth-moving memoir through Tolstoi's railway planning in the 1920s and the wartime logistics work of Hitchcock, Kantorovich, and Koopmans in the 1940s, which made it a linear program; Dantzig's simplex gave it an algorithm in 1949. Analysts revived it in the 1990s, Brenier's theorem above all, while computer vision renamed it the earth mover's distance. In parallel, transportation science had already invented entropic regularization as Wilson's 1969 gravity model, and the rescaling iterations reach back through Sinkhorn 1964 to Kruithof 1937 and Yule 1912. Benamou and Brenier's fluid formulation (2000), the Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto flow (1998), and Cuturi's 2013 Sinkhorn revival for machine learning complete the genealogy this book consolidates.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors model the reader as a data scientist who meets distributions as data and needs geometry that computes. Their conviction is that theory earns its place only when it guides the design of an algorithm: duality is taught because it yields solvers and certificates, Brenier because it yields maps and interpolations, contraction theory because it yields stopping rules. The three-layer exposition, histograms first, then discrete measures, then arbitrary measures in gray boxes, assumes the reader will implement the finite version and consult the general one. Every figure is reproducible from companion code, which states their epistemic standard plainly: a claim about transport should ship with the computation that exhibits it.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results in this book veto moves other layers of a system might want to make. Mass conservation vetoes any comparison that quietly renormalizes unequal totals away; the unbalanced theory must be invoked explicitly, with its exchange rate tau declared. The sample complexity results veto high-dimensional plug-in Wasserstein estimates from small samples: the noise floor is computable and binding. The non-Hilbertian theorem vetoes feeding Wasserstein distance matrices to kernel machines as if they were Euclidean. Complementary slackness vetoes explanations whose prices disagree with the plan they explain. And the epsilon analysis vetoes reporting a regularized transport value without its epsilon and its debiasing, because the raw number mixes geometry with self-transport bias.

universal_lens: Optimal transport is the general template for comparing any two structured piles of stuff when rearrangement has a price: define the ground cost of moving one unit, impose conservation, and the least-cost rearrangement becomes a distance with a dual price system attached. The same schema audits supply chains against demand, morphs one shape into another, aligns vocabularies across languages, and interpolates between physical states. Its companion lesson is symmetric: whenever a comparison ignores the cost of rearrangement and only checks overlap, it will call near things far and far things identical. Conservation plus ground geometry plus duality is a reusable grammar for honest comparison in any domain where mass, count, or probability must be accounted for.
gsi_mapping: The Institute takes the monograph as core methods curriculum for reasoning about distributions. Its durable exports are habits of proof and audit: dual certificates before trusting a computed distance, contraction-based stopping rules instead of iteration folklore, explicit epsilon and tau declarations on every regularized quantity, and sample-complexity budgets attached to every empirical claim. The Laguerre tessellation and the Kantorovich-Rubinstein witness supply its model of an explanation: a partition of the space into owned regions, or a bounded-slope critic function that shows where two distributions differ. The negative results are curriculum too, since knowing that a geometry cannot be kernelized, or that a rate is dimension-cursed, is what separates a research institute's claims from numerology.
gse_mapping: The engine takes a layered comparison stack. Screening questions (did this unit's distribution change?) run on MMD or sliced Wasserstein for their dimension-free or sorting-based cost. Measurement questions (how far, and where?) run on debiased Sinkhorn divergences with declared epsilon, exact network simplex certificates for small cases, and Kantorovich potentials as the per-state attribution of every reported distance. Consensus objects (a class of opponents, a typical week) are Wasserstein barycenters; roster churn and unequal play counts route to unbalanced transport with a declared tau; cross-space structural analogy routes to Gromov-Wasserstein, labeled as hypothesis. Simulator fitting uses minimum Kantorovich estimation with coupling gradients, and every distance ships with its sample-complexity noise floor.
